The brick basin is the longest straight Harappan structure at Lothal and its two long walls (each about 215 m) give the most precise direction on the site. The town walls west of it are faint and short, but they agree with the basin within their errors, so the basin stands for the layout of the whole excavated settlement.

The eastern fortification is the longest Harappan line on the plan with exposed stretches along its length, and the 1983-84 plan gives the same direction for it within about one degree. The other sides of the circuit are drawn largely as conjecture and are not square to it, and the streets run obliquely, so Banawali has no single orthogonal layout to report.

It contains the longest measured line, the street drain, and the walls that line the main street through the excavated part of Mound II, which is the layout the rest of the excavated buildings follow most closely.

The contour plan is the only measured plan whose north is defined by a geographic graticule rather than a drawn arrow, and its castle and Middle Town edges agree with each other within about one degree. The three drafted plans place the same walls six to eight degrees to either side of their own arrows, so their arrows, not the walls, are the uncertain element.
Main Street, both lanes and most of the walls of all three structure complexes share this direction, which is square within about one degree; the second group is confined to some rooms of Complex 3.
The periphery wall is the only long Harappan line on the published plan; the brick walls inside it in trenches Do10-Do11 follow its two arms.

The Great Granary on Mound F is the most regular rectilinear building at Harappa and its long walls are the straightest measured lines on any of the plans; the citadel walls form a parallelogram whose long sides and south side do not share one direction, so they cannot stand for a single layout.

The street blocks of the lower city are the planned layout of the town. On the 1967-68 plan their edges are square to each other within about two degrees, and the independently drawn 1968-69 plan gives the same direction for the same streets relative to its own north (sys5) within one degree.

The fort wall is the only measurable Harappan architecture on the plan; its two long exposed arms are square to each other within about two degrees and the shorter stretches on the other two sides agree with them within a few degrees.

The dock is the longest straight Harappan structure at Lothal and is drawn as excavated on the only measured plan of the whole town; the town plan's acropolis edges agree with it within a few degrees. The two excavation figures give local systems for the warehouse and for one house block, each relative to its own drawn rose.

First Street is the longest straight street of the lower town and the spine of both excavated areas we measured. On Marshall's HR plan its west frontage and drain give the best-controlled direction (the plan's meridian is long and ruled); on Mackay's DK-G plan the two sides of First Street and Central Street (sys8) agree with it within about two degrees, but that plan's north arrow is only 46 px long.
The long wall of RGP-4 is the longest measured line at Rangpur and the walls of room 11 agree with it; room 19 in RGP-2 lies close to the same direction relative to its own rose.
It is the only plan of Rojdi with a north arrow and measurable walls; the north wall, the longest and straightest, carries most of the weight.
The citadel ramparts are the longest straight lines at the site and frame the whole settlement; the annexe rampart and houses follow nearly the same direction.
